steps.title: Safe casts and smart casts
steps.body:
**as?** is a **safe cast**: it returns the value if the type matches and **null** otherwise, instead of crashing like **as**.

After an **is** check, Kotlin **smart casts** the variable, so you can use it as the checked type without writing a cast.

steps.title: let, elvis and early exits
steps.body: **?.let { }** runs a block only when the value is **not null**. The **?:** operator can also hold **return** or **throw**, which makes guard clauses short: val n = input ?: return.

steps.title: as? with safe call and elvis

notes.text: as? gives null for non-strings; ?. skips the call; ?: supplies 0.
A String passes the cast, so its length is used.
An Int fails the safe cast and falls back to 0.
null also falls back to 0.

steps.title: Smart casts with is

notes.text: Inside the if, x is automatically a String.
Here x is smart cast to a List.
Anything else returns -1.

steps.title: let for non-null work

notes.text: The block runs because name is not null; it is the block parameter.
The block is skipped when the value is null.
Safe call plus elvis gives a default.

steps.question: What does as? return when the cast is impossible?
steps.explanation: The safe cast operator yields null instead of throwing.

steps.question: What does this print?
steps.explanation: The String cannot be cast to Int, so as? gives null.

steps.title: Ranges
steps.body: **1..5** is a closed range, **1 until 5** excludes the end, **10 downTo 1** counts down and **step** changes the stride. Use **in** and **!in** to test membership, even for characters like 'a'..'e'.

steps.title: when and immutability
steps.body:
**when** can match values, ranges (**in**), types (**is**) or arbitrary conditions with no subject. It is an expression, so every case must produce a value.

**val** fixes the reference, but a **MutableList** held in a val can still change its contents.

steps.title: Range tools
steps.code:
fun main() {
    println((1..5).toList())
    println((1 until 5).toList())
    println((10 downTo 1 step 3).toList())
    println(3 in 1..5)
    println('c' in 'a'..'e')
}

notes.text: A closed range includes both ends.
until stops before the end.
downTo with step counts down by 3.
in tests membership.

steps.title: when without a subject
steps.code:
fun classify(x: Any): String = when {
    x == 0 -> "zero"
    x is Int && x in 1..9 -> "digit"
    x is Int -> "big int"
    x is String -> "text of ${x.length}"
    else -> "other"
}

fun main() {
    println(classify(0))
    println(classify(7))
    println(classify(100))
    println(classify("hey"))
    println(classify(2.5))
}

notes.text: Each branch is a condition; the first true one wins.
After x is Int, x is smart cast so in 1..9 compiles.
The String branch uses its length.
else catches everything left.

steps.output:
zero
digit
big int
text of 3
other

steps.title: val with a mutable collection
steps.code:
fun main() {
    val list = mutableListOf(1, 2)
    list.add(3)
    var total = 0
    for (n in list) total += n
    println(list)
    println(total)
}

notes.text: The reference is val but the list itself is mutable.
total is a var so it can change.
The list now holds three items.

steps.question: Can you add to a val mutableListOf()?
options: Yes, only the reference is fixed
steps.explanation: val prevents reassigning the variable, not changing a mutable collection.

steps.title: Transform, filter, reduce
steps.body:
**map** transforms each item, **filter** keeps matches, **fold(initial)** combines items with a starting value and **reduce** combines without one.

**groupBy** builds a Map of lists, **zip** pairs two lists and **partition** splits by a condition.

steps.title: Lazy sequences
steps.body: A **Sequence** processes items **one at a time** and only when a **terminal operation** like toList() runs. That avoids building big intermediate lists and works with infinite sources such as **generateSequence**.

steps.title: map, filter, fold, reduce
steps.code:
fun main() {
    val nums = listOf(1, 2, 3, 4, 5)
    println(nums.map { it * it })
    println(nums.filter { it % 2 == 1 })
    println(nums.fold(10) { acc, n -> acc + n })
    println(nums.reduce { a, b -> a * b })
}

notes.text: it is the single lambda parameter.
Keeps only odd numbers.
fold starts at 10 and adds every number.
reduce multiplies all numbers: 5 factorial.

steps.title: groupBy, zip, associateWith, partition
steps.code:
fun main() {
    val words = listOf("apple", "avocado", "banana", "blueberry", "cherry")
    println(words.groupBy { it.first() })
    println(words.zip(listOf(1, 2, 3)))
    println(words.associateWith { it.length }["banana"])
    println(words.partition { it.length > 6 })
}

notes.text: Groups words by their first letter.
zip stops at the shorter list.
associateWith builds a Map from word to length.
partition returns a pair of lists.

steps.output:
{a=[apple, avocado], b=[banana, blueberry], c=[cherry]}
[(apple, 1), (avocado, 2), (banana, 3)]
6
([avocado, blueberry], [apple, banana, cherry])

steps.title: Extension functions
steps.body:
An **extension function** adds a function to an existing type without inheriting from it: fun String.exclaim() = this + "!".

Inside, **this** is the **receiver** object.

steps.title: Lambdas and function types
steps.body:
A function type is written **(Int) -> Int**. Lambdas are values you can store, pass and return. If a lambda is the **last argument**, it can go outside the parentheses.

Lambdas **capture** variables from their surroundings (closures).

steps.title: Extension functions
steps.code:
fun String.exclaim(): String = this + "!"

fun Int.isEven(): Boolean = this % 2 == 0

fun main() {
    println("hey".exclaim())
    println(4.isEven())
    println(7.isEven())
}

notes.text: String is the receiver type and this is the string.
Extensions work on primitives too.
Call it like a normal member.

notes.text: f is a parameter whose type is a function.
A trailing lambda goes after the parentheses.
A lambda stored in a val.
Pass the same value to map.

notes.text: The function returns another function.
count lives on inside the returned lambda.

steps.title: Interfaces
steps.body: An **interface** declares functions and properties that classes **implement**. Interfaces may include default implementations, and a class can implement several.

steps.title: object, companion and data
steps.body:
An **object** is a **singleton**. A **companion object** holds members that belong to the class itself, such as factory functions.

A **data class** adds equals, hashCode, toString, copy and **destructuring** automatically.

steps.title: Interface with a default

notes.text: Implementers must provide area.
describe has a default body that calls area.
override supplies the required member.

steps.title: Singleton and companion

notes.text: An object is created once and used by name.
The constructor is private; use the factory.
The companion lives on the class.
next++ returns the old value then increments.

steps.title: Data classes
steps.code:
data class Book(val title: String, val pages: Int)

fun main() {
    val b = Book("Kotlin", 300)
    val (title, pages) = b
    println("$title has $pages pages")
    println(b.copy(pages = 350))
    println(setOf(b, Book("Kotlin", 300)).size)
}

notes.text: Destructuring uses the generated component functions.
copy changes only the named property.
equals and hashCode make the two books the same set element.

steps.question: What does a companion object hold?
options: Members that belong to the class itself
steps.explanation: Companion members are called on the class name, like static members.

steps.title: Closed hierarchies
steps.body:
A **sealed class** or **sealed interface** limits which subclasses can exist: all direct subclasses are known at compile time.

That makes **when** over a sealed type **exhaustive**: the compiler checks every case and no else branch is needed.

steps.title: Modelling state
steps.body:
Sealed types are ideal for **UI state**, **results** and **expression trees**. Each subclass can carry its own data: Success holds a value, Failure holds a reason and Loading holds nothing.

Note: sealed interface needs Kotlin 1.5 or newer.

steps.title: A sealed class for state

notes.text: Subclasses are declared inside the sealed class.
object suits a case with no data.
No else is needed because the cases are exhaustive.
Smart cast gives access to value.

steps.title: A sealed interface

notes.text: A sealed interface works like a sealed class but allows multiple inheritance.
Both implementations are covered.
3.0 stands in for pi to keep numbers simple.

steps.title: enum versus sealed

notes.text: An enum has fixed constant instances.
Every constant has a name and an ordinal.
valueOf looks up a constant by its name.

steps.question: Why does when over a sealed type not need else?
options: All direct subclasses are known, so the compiler checks coverage
Sealed types have only one subclass
steps.explanation: The compiler knows every possible subtype.

steps.explanation: The argument is a B instance.

steps.title: Five scope functions
steps.body:
**let** and **run** return the lambda result; **apply** and **also** return the object itself. **let** and **also** call the object **it**; **run**, **apply** and **with** use **this**.

Use **apply** to configure an object, **let** for null checks, **also** for side effects like logging.

steps.title: Generics
steps.body: A **type parameter** such as **T** lets one class or function work with many types: class Box<T>. A **constraint** like T : Comparable<T> restricts which types are allowed and unlocks their members.

steps.title: let, run, with, apply and also

notes.text: apply configures the object and returns it.
let hands the object in as it and returns the block result.
with uses the object as this.
also returns p, then run reads age through this.

steps.output:
Person(name=Ada, age=37)
Ada (37)
Ada is 37
also: Ada
37

notes.text: T is inferred from the arguments.
A generic class stores a value of any type.
T became String.
T became Double.

steps.title: Generic constraints

notes.text: T must be Comparable, so > works.
Strings compare alphabetically.

steps.explanation: apply uses this as the receiver and returns the object.

steps.title: Coroutines
steps.body:
A **coroutine** is a lightweight task that can **suspend** without blocking a thread. A **suspend** function can call **delay** or other suspend functions. **launch** starts a task, **async** returns a result with **await**, and **runBlocking** bridges normal code.

The examples in this chapter need the kotlinx.coroutines library, so read them here; the basic online sandbox has only the standard library.

steps.title: Flow
steps.body:
A **Flow** is a **cold** asynchronous stream: nothing runs until something calls **collect**. Operators like **map** and **filter** transform values as they arrive.

In Android, **StateFlow** holds the latest UI state and **structured concurrency** cancels child work when its scope ends.

steps.title: launch and runBlocking

notes.text: runBlocking runs coroutines inside a normal main.
launch starts a child coroutine without waiting.
delay suspends without blocking the thread.
This line runs first, so hello prints before world.

steps.title: async and await

notes.text: suspend marks a function that may pause.
Both async blocks start immediately and run concurrently.
await collects each result: 2 plus 4.

steps.title: A cold Flow

notes.text: flow builds a stream but does not run yet.
emit sends a value downstream.
collect starts the flow and receives each mapped value.

steps.question: What does suspend mean on a function?
options: It can pause without blocking its thread
steps.explanation: Suspending functions can be paused and resumed by the coroutine machinery.

steps.question: What does it mean that a Flow is cold?
options: Nothing runs until it is collected
steps.explanation: A cold flow starts producing when a collector subscribes.

examples.title: Kotlin: Sealed Classes
examples.code:
sealed class Expr
data class Num(val value: Int) : Expr()
data class Add(val left: Expr, val right: Expr) : Expr()
data class Mul(val left: Expr, val right: Expr) : Expr()

fun eval(e: Expr): Int = when (e) {
    is Num -> e.value
    is Add -> eval(e.left) + eval(e.right)
    is Mul -> eval(e.left) * eval(e.right)
}

fun main() {
    val expr = Add(Num(2), Mul(Num(3), Num(4)))
    println(eval(expr))
    println(expr)
}
